extracted.intended_audience: pop-culture readers, comedy fans, and media/ethics observers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating when and how comedians may embellish stories versus when factual accuracy is required—especially for stories about racism, law enforcement, or real people—and how journalists should report and fact-check those claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy for true stories about racism and Islamophobia
rubrics_metrics.description: How much accuracy is required from comics who say they are telling true stories about racism, social issues and real people; being accused of 'fake racism' is serious and 'not trivial.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the comic's account conveys factual events or creates false impressions about experiencing racism/Islamophobia. Examples: prom-rejection story (whether rejection was race-motivated), claims about encounters with an FBI informant, and other personal allegations. False or misleading claims on these topics can damage credibility and harm broader causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-specific factual standard (political comedy vs comedic storytelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction stated on the record: 'In political comedy, facts come first. In comedic storytelling, emotions come first.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply differing standards depending on format: hold political/commercial journalism-style material to higher factual standards; allow more emotional/poetic license in clearly narrative/storytelling comedy, but still flag serious factual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide evidence and context for factual claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Creators should supply evidence and contextual information when making factual claims; Minhaj presented emails and text messages to support his version of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a performer asserts specific factual events (dates, communications, interactions), corroborating documents, witnesses, or contemporary records strengthen credibility. Lack of provided evidence makes claims more vulnerable to fact-checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic fact-checking and sourcing standards
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should carefully report and fact-check pieces, including interviews with multiple people and presenting the subject's perspective at length: 'Our piece... was carefully reported and fact-checked. It is based on interviews with more than 20 people... We stand by our story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess articles based on the depth and breadth of sourcing, whether subjects and relevant people were interviewed, and transparency about methods. Strong journalistic practice includes corroboration and allowing subjects to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid eliding or concocting details to center oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique that performers 'elided or concocted other details in his stories, often to place himself more squarely at the center of the action.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for narrative moves that unjustifiably reposition the storyteller at the center of events; verify whether details are added or shifted to increase dramatic centrality (examples cited: timing of a meeting, fabricated seating anecdotes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and apology for embellishment when it misleads
rubrics_metrics.description: Comics should acknowledge embellishments and apologize if those embellishments misled people or caused harm: Minhaj says 'I am sorry for embellishing the story, if anyone was worrying about me and my family.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When exaggeration crosses into misleading territory—especially on serious topics—public acknowledgment and correction help mitigate harm. Evaluate whether the apology addresses the central factual concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensationalizing potentially dangerous incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Be precise and responsible when recounting incidents that could be construed as dangerous (example: receiving an envelope with white powder that was not anthrax and did not spill or cause a hospital trip).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dramatize health/safety incidents beyond what evidence supports. Misrepresenting risk can cause unnecessary alarm and undermine trust in other legitimate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect anonymity while maintaining clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pseudonyms or anonymization to protect individuals (Minhaj calls the woman in the prom story 'Bethany' to protect her anonymity) but don't let anonymity obscure key facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymization is appropriate to protect privacy, but creators should still provide enough corroborating detail or context for claims to be assessable; journalists should note when anonymity limits verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronological and factual specificity (dates/timing matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate timing and sequence are important (examples: whether a meeting at an embassy occurred as news broke or a month earlier).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check dates and chronology; misplacing events in time can change interpretation and be an indicator of embellishment or error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing comedic license against potential harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Comics may exaggerate for a punchline, but there's a threshold where exaggeration is not OK—especially when it involves real people's experiences or sensitive topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the seriousness of the subject, the likelihood of real-world harm (reputational, legal, or to social causes), and audience expectation of truth when deciding whether a comedic exaggeration is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider reputational and career consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims and fact-checking can have high stakes for a performer's reputation and opportunities (article notes Minhaj was a front runner for The Daily Show host and later informed he will not be getting the job).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing material, consider downstream effects on career and relationships; integrity and accuracy affect hiring and public trust.
